'''Shyamala Gopalan Harris'''{{Efn|As per the cited sources and the common [[Indian name#Tamil|naming conventions]] of her family, Gopalan Shyamala was her legal name in India,<ref name=uscis>{{cite web|url=https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/foia/Shyamala_Gopalan_Harris.pdf|title=Shyamala_Gopalan_Harris.pdf|publisher=[[United States Citizenship and Immigration Services]]|access-date=2024-03-23|page=14/154|quote=Gopalan Shyamala [Maiden]}}<br>Also see: {{cite web|url=https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/foia/Shyamala_Gopalan_Harris.pdf|title=Shyamala_Gopalan_Harris.pdf|publisher=[[United States Citizenship and Immigration Services]]|access-date=2024-03-23|page=23/154}} which is an Indian government document that uses the form "G. Shyamala".</ref> while Shyamala Gopalan conforms to [[Western name order]]. Shyamala Gopalan Harris, as the first, middle and last names, was her legal name in the United States.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/foia/Shyamala_Gopalan_Harris.pdf|title=Shyamala_Gopalan_Harris.pdf|publisher=[[United States Citizenship and Immigration Services]]|access-date=2024-03-23|page=8/154}}</ref> In some U.S. government documents, she placed her given name in the surname field and her patronymic in the given name field. She worked jobs under her maiden name even after she married.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/foia/Shyamala_Gopalan_Harris.pdf|title=Shyamala_Gopalan_Harris.pdf|publisher=[[United States Citizenship and Immigration Services]]|access-date=2024-03-23|page=90/154}}</ref>}} ([[Birth name|née]] '''Gopalan'''; December 7, 1938 – February 11, 2009) was an Indian-born American [[biomedical scientist]] at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]],<ref name=tabasko-harris>{{citation|last=Tabasko|first=Michael|journal=NIH Catalyst |publisher=National Institutes of Health, Office of the Director|volume=29|issue=4|pages=1, 6|date=July–August 2021|title=A Fortuitious Connection: Vice President Kamala Harris's Mother and Her NIH Collaborations|url=https://irp.nih.gov/system/files/media/file/2022-01/v29i4-NIH-Catalyst_JULY-AUGUST-2021_3.pdf|quote=Gopalan eventually left Canada and returned to California to continue her work on the role of hormone receptors in breast-cancer development at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley, California). She was awarded several NIH grants supporting her research through 2001, and her lab published their findings in 2006 (Cancer Res 66:10391–10398, 2006). (Photo caption: Shyamala Gopalan Harris (left) in her lab at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.)}}</ref>  whose work in isolating and characterizing the [[progesterone receptor]] gene has stimulated advances in breast biology and [[oncology]].<ref name="bcaction" /> She was the mother of [[Kamala Harris]], the former [[Vice President of the United States|vice president of the United States]] who also served as [[Attorney General of California|attorney general of California]] and senator, and [[Maya Harris]], a [[lawyer]] and [[political commentator]].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Cadelago |first1=Christopher |last2=Oprysko |first2=Caitlin |title=Biden picks Kamala Harris as VP nominee |date=August 11, 2020 |publisher=Politico |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2020/08/11/joe-biden-vp-pick-kamala-harris-393768 |accessdate=August 31, 2020}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Shyamala was born on December 7, 1938, in [[Madras]], British India to [[Iyengar]] parents, [[P. V. Gopalan|Painganadu Venkataraman Gopalan]], a [[civil servant]], and Gopalan Rajam (née Balachandran), her mother. Her parents were from two villages near the town of [[Mannargudi]] in [[Madras Province]].<ref name="LATimes_stenographer">{{citation |last1 = Bengali |first1 =Shashank |last2=Mason |first2=Melanie |url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2019-10-25/how-kamala-harris-indian-family-shaped-her-political-career |title=The progressive Indian grandfather who inspired Kamala Harris | work=Los Angeles Times |date=25 October 2019 |accessdate=24 April 2020 |quote=He started out as a stenographer, and moved the family from New Delhi to Mumbai to Kolkata as he climbed the ranks of the civil service.}}</ref> Gopalan had begun his professional life as a [[stenographer]],<ref name="LATimes_stenographer"/> and, as he rose through the ranks of the [[Imperial Secretariat Service]] and later [[Central Secretariat Service]],<ref name="Gazette 34 1956">{{cite web |title=Gazette of India, 1956, No. 34 (Archived)|page=56 |url=https://archive.org/details/in.gazette.1956.34/page/n7/mode/2up |work=[[Government of India]] |date=1956-02-04 |access-date=2024-07-27 |quote=No, A-5(16)/55.—The services of Shri P. V. Gopalan, permanent Grade I officer of the Central Secretariat Service and employed as Under Secretary in the Ministry of Transport (Roads Wing), were placed at the disposal of the Ministry of Rehabilitation with effect from the 31st December, 1955 (A.N.)}}</ref> he moved the family every few years between Madras (now [[Chennai]]), [[New Delhi]], Bombay (now [[Mumbai]]), and Calcutta (now [[Kolkata]]).<ref name="LATimes_stenographer"/> He and Rajam had an [[arranged marriage]], but according to Shyamala's brother, Balachandran, their parents were broad-minded in raising the children, all of whom led somewhat unconventional lives.<ref name="LATimes_stenographer"/> A gifted singer of [[Carnatic music]], Shyamala won a national competition in it as a teenager.<ref name="LATimes_stenographer"/>

Shyamala went to the [[Delhi Tamil Education Association Senior Secondary Schools|MEA school]] in Delhi and received her [[Higher Secondary Certificate]] in 1955.<ref name=uscis /> She studied for a [[Bachelor of Science]] in [[Home Science]] at [[Lady Irwin College]], [[University of Delhi]]. Her father thought the subject—which taught skills considered helpful in homemaking—was a mismatch for her abilities; her mother expected the children to seek careers in medicine, engineering, or law.<ref name="LATimes_stenographer"/> In 1958, aged 19, Shyamala unexpectedly applied to the master's program in [[Nutritional science|nutrition]] and [[endocrinology]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and was accepted. Her parents used some of their retirement savings to pay her tuition and board during the first year.<ref name="LATimes_stenographer"/> Lacking a phone line at home, they communicated with her by [[aerogram]] after she arrived in the U.S. She earned a [[Ph.D.]] in nutrition and endocrinology at UC Berkeley in 1964.<ref name="LATimes_stenographer"/> Shyamala's dissertation, which was supervised by Richard L. Lyman,<ref name="lyman">{{cite book|last=Gopalan |first=Shyamala |date=1964 |title=The isolation and purification of a trypsin inhibitor from whole-wheat flour |publisher=University of California}}</ref> was titled ''The isolation and purification of a [[trypsin]] inhibitor from whole wheat flour''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Shyamala |first=Gopalan |date=1964 |title=The isolation and purification of a trypsin inhibitor from whole-wheat flour |url=http://oskicat.berkeley.edu/record=b14935598~S1 |publisher=UC Berkeley}} Note: her given name "Shyamala" is put in the last name field, while her [[patronymic]] (father's name), "Gopalan", is put in the first name field. The name form given is "Shyamala, Gopalan".</ref>

== Career ==
Shyamala conducted research in UC Berkeley's Department of Physiology and Cancer Research Lab. She worked as a breast cancer researcher at [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]] and [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|University of Wisconsin]]. She worked for 16 years at [[Lady Davis Institute for Medical Research]] and [[McGill University Faculty of Medicine]]. She served as a peer reviewer for the [[National Institutes of Health]] and as a site visit team member for the Federal Advisory Committee. She also served on the President's Special Commission on Breast Cancer. She mentored dozens of students in her lab. For her last decade of research, Shyamala worked in the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. G. Shyamala |url=http://crea.berkeley.edu/shyamala-profile.shtml |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190123171257/http://crea.berkeley.edu/shyamala-profile.shtml |archive-date=2019-01-23 |access-date=2024-08-09 }}</ref>

=== Research ===
Shyamala's research led to advancements in the knowledge of [[hormone]]s pertaining to [[breast cancer]].<ref name="montreal" /><ref name="bcaction" /> Her work in the isolation and characterization of the progesterone receptor gene in mice changed research on the hormone-responsiveness of [[breast tissue]].<ref name="bcaction" />

== Personal life ==
In the fall of 1962, at a meeting of the [[Afro-American Association]]—a students' group at Berkeley whose members would go on to give structure to the discipline of [[Black studies]], propose the holiday of [[Kwanzaa]], and help establish the [[Black Panther Party]]—Shyamala met a graduate student in economics from [[Jamaica]], [[Donald J. Harris]], who was that day's speaker.<ref name=NYTimes-9-13-2020>{{citation | last = Barry |first =Ellen |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/09/13/us/kamala-harris-parents.html| title=How Kamala Harris's Immigrant Parents Found a Home, and Each Other, in a Black Study Group | work=New York Times | date=13 September 2020 | accessdate=13 September 2020}}</ref> According to Donald Harris, who is later an [[emeritus professor]] of economics at [[Stanford University]], "We talked then, continued to talk at a subsequent meeting, and at another, and another."<ref name=NYTimes-9-13-2020/> In 1963, they were married without following the convention of introducing Harris to Shyamala's parents beforehand or having the ceremony in her hometown.<ref name="LATimes_stenographer"/> In the later 1960s, Donald and Shyamala took their daughters, Kamala, then four or five years old, and Maya, two years younger, to newly independent [[Zambia]], where Shyamala's father, P. V. Gopalan, was on an advisory assignment.<ref name="LATimes_stenographer"/> After Shyamala and Donald divorced in the early 1970s, she took her daughters to India several times to visit her parents in [[Chennai]], where they had retired.<ref name="LATimes_stenographer"/><ref>{{cite news|last1=Finnegan|first1=Michael|title=How race helped shape the politics of Senate candidate Kamala Harris|url=https://www.latimes.com/local/politics/la-me-pol-ca-harris-senate-20150930-story.html|accessdate=December 1, 2018|work=Los Angeles Times|date=September 30, 2015}}</ref>

The children also visited their father's family in [[Jamaica]] during their childhood.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Dolan|first1=Casey|title=How Kamala Harris' immigrant parents shaped her life—and her political outlook|url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/10/kamala-harris-president-parents-shyamala-gopalan-donald-harris-berkeley/|accessdate=August 14, 2020|work=The Mercury News|date=February 10, 2019}}</ref>

==Death ==
Shyamala died of [[colon cancer]] in Oakland on February 11, 2009, at age 70.<ref name="bcaction" /> She requested that donations be made to the organization [[Breast Cancer Action]].<ref name="bcaction" /> Later in 2009, Kamala Harris carried her mother's ashes to [[Chennai]] on the southeastern coast of [[peninsular India]] and dispersed them in the [[Indian Ocean]] waters.<ref>{{cite news | last1 = Gettleman |first1 = Jeffrey |last2=Raj |first2=Suhasini|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/08/16/world/asia/kamala-harris-india.html | title=How Kamala Harris's Family in India Helped Shape Her Values| work=New York Times | date=16 August 2020 | accessdate=17 August 2020|quote=One sunny morning, Ms. Harris and her uncle walked down to the beach in Besant Nagar where she used to stroll with her grandfather all those years ago, and scattered the ashes on the waves.}}</ref>

Shyamala Gopalan's legacy lives on through her cancer research, social advocacy, and the [[Shyamala Gopalan Educational Foundation]], which advances education, healthcare, sustainability, and community welfare across India.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-08-08 |title=From Ruins to Reverence: Nalla Suresh Reddy Revives Kakatiya-Era Temple in Tribute to Dr. Shyamala Gopalan Harris |url=https://www.thehindu.com/brandhub/from-ruins-to-reverence-nalla-suresh-reddy-revives-kakatiya-era-temple-in-tribute-to-dr-shyamala-gopalan-harris/article69910240.ece |access-date=2025-08-12 |work=The Hindu |language=en-IN |issn=0971-751X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Today |first=Telangana |date=2022-07-02 |title=US delegation visits Shyamala Gopalan Foundation office in Kothagudem |url=https://telanganatoday.com/us-delegation-visits-shyamala-gopalan-foundation-office-in-kothagudem |access-date=2025-08-12 |website=Telangana Today |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-12-07 |title=Shyamala Gopalan birth anniversary: SGEF foundation provides Rs 5 lakh life cover to 500 families |url=https://www.timesnownews.com/india/shyamala-gopalan-birth-anniversary-sgef-foundation-provides-rs-5-lakh-life-cover-to-500-families-article-96063390 |access-date=2025-08-12 |website=Times Now |language=en}}</ref>
